## 1. General information

| Field | Proposed specification |
|---|---|
| Course code | MLB7052.LT |
| Course title | Kaasaegsed meetodid molekulaarses ökoloogias / Modern Molecular Methods in Ecology |
| Semester | 2026/2027 autumn |
| Language | Estonian teaching; English reading and software documentation |
| Credits | 10 ECTS, proposed expansion from 6 ECTS |
| Contact hours | 102 hours: lectures, seminars, demonstrations, and practicals |
| Independent work | 158 hours |
| Prerequisites | MLK6922.LT Biochemistry; MLB6013.LT Genetics |
| Lecturer | Peeter Laas |
| Assessment | Graded: A, B, C, D, E, F |
| Intended audience | Advanced undergraduate and master's students in molecular ecology, biology, biotechnology, and related fields |

::: {style="margin-top:1em; font-size:0.78em; color:#777;"}
Empty folder → 35 slides → shinyapps.io · `r temp`°C in Tartu at render time
:::

---

##  Course purpose

::: {.incremental}
1. understand the molecular principles behind DNA, RNA, proteins, genomes, gene expression, and molecular phenotypes;
2. understand the strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate uses of major molecular methods in ecology and evolutionary biology;
3. develop practical competence in sample design, nucleic-acid extraction, quantification, PCR, electrophoresis, sequencing, and basic computational analysis;
4. learn to connect molecular observations with ecological interactions, population structure, phylogeny, and environmental change;
5. develop reproducible habits for controls, contamination prevention, metadata, quality assessment, and scientific reporting;
6. design an end-to-end molecular study and defend the limitations of the proposed inference.
:::

---

## The main aim

The course develops a working understanding of molecular biology and its use in ecological and evolutionary research. Students move from the molecular basis of information to a defensible study design:

**biological question -> sample -> molecule -> assay -> sequence or measurement -> computation -> inference**

::: {.notes}
The goal isn't to replace thinking — it's to reduce friction. You still need to understand the code.
:::

---

# The course

---

## 5. Course content {.scrollable}

::: {.dropdown-table}

<details>
<summary><strong>Block I</strong> — Foundations and measurement</summary>

- evolution, scientific reasoning, and molecular biology as a way of knowing;
- chemical properties of DNA, RNA, proteins, buffers, enzymes, and molecular interactions;
- information flow, replication, mutation, repair, recombination, transcription, translation, and regulation;
- sample representativeness, preservation, extraction, quantification, inhibition, and contamination.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Block II</strong> — The molecular toolkit</summary>

- electrophoresis, restriction analysis, Southern blotting, PCR, qPCR, ddPCR, Sanger sequencing, probes, FISH, fluorescence, and flow cytometry;
- molecular markers, barcoding, metabarcoding, allozymes, RFLP, microsatellites, and SNPs;
- Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, library preparation, read quality, assembly, annotation, and data management.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Block III</strong> — Genomes and molecular phenotypes</summary>

- comparative genomics, assembly, annotation, and public sequence databases;
- transcriptomics, non-coding RNA, stage- and condition-specific regulation, epigenetics, and functional genomics;
- proteomics, quantitative proteomics, protein interactions, post-translational modification, and molecular phenotypes;
- the cell biology behind the traits we measure: life-cycle stages, secretion, transport, and cellular responses to the environment.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Block IV</strong> — Ecology, evolution, and application</summary>

- phylogeny, phylogeography, population genetics, coalescence, and community-level inference;
- species interactions, symbiosis, host-associated microbiota, and environmental monitoring;
- CRISPR, LAMP, microfluidics, lab-on-chip, biosensing, and field-deployable diagnostics;
- an integrated student capstone from question to inference.

</details>

:::

## Copilot limits

```r
# number of timesteps to iterate the model
t_max = 10
# initial population size
N0 = 20
# population growth rate
r = 0.2
# initialise an empty vector to store the population size

# over time
Ns = numeric(t_max+1)
# set the population size in the first timestep to N0
Ns[1] = N0
# execute a loop from time t=1 to t=t_max, iterating the

for (t in 1:t_max)
Ns[t+1] = (1+r)*Ns[t]
# plot the results
plot(0:t_max,Ns,pch=19,type='o',xlab='t',ylab='N',
ylim=c(0,max(Ns)))
```

## 10. Responsible use of AI

AI tools may be used for brainstorming, terminology support, code explanation, language editing, and generating candidate analysis plans. Students remain responsible for factual accuracy, citations, code correctness, data provenance, and the final interpretation. AI-generated text or code used in a submitted assignment must be declared briefly. AI must not be used to fabricate observations, replace required practical work, or conceal the origin of an analysis.

## 12. Administrative implementation note

The existing 6 ECTS course can be retained as a compact version by selecting Weeks 1-8, 13, and 15, retaining the current practical sequence, and reducing the capstone. The 10 ECTS version should be adopted only after the timetable, laboratory capacity, staffing, assessment load, and programme-level credit requirements have been confirmed.
## What you can now ask Claude Code

With R connected as MCP:


## Saving tokens — why it matters

LLM APIs charge per token. A sloppy workflow burns money fast:

| Habit | Approx tokens |
|---|---|
| link | https://www.stt.msu.edu/~melfi/STT180Text/classification.html#knn-and-the-iris-data |
| `btw(my_df)` — one data frame | 200–600 |
| Pasting entire help page | 3,000–8,000 |
| `btw_tool_docs_help_page("pkg","fn")` | 400–1,200 |
| Re-explaining project context every session | 500–2,000 |
| `CLAUDE.md` project file (read once) | 200–500 |

**Rule: describe only what the model needs to answer this specific question.**

---

## Token-saving techniques with btw

```r
# app.R version 1

library(shiny)

names.df <- read.csv("https://www.finley-lab.com/files/data/name_list.csv")

# Define UI
ui <- fluidPage(
  
  titlePanel("Random Names Analysis"),
  
  sidebarLayout(
    
    sidebarPanel("our inputs will be here"),
    
    mainPanel("our output will appear here")
  )
)

# Define server logic
server <- function(input, output) {}

# Create Shiny app
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

## CLAUDE.md — your project memory

Create a `CLAUDE.md` file in your project root. Claude Code reads it at every session start — **you never re-explain your project**.

```markdown
# CLAUDE.md

## Project
EEA bathing water quality analysis, 1990–2024.
Main data: data/bw_assessment_eea_datahub_1990_2024_data.csv (672k rows)

## Key columns
- `countryCode`: ISO2 country code
- `season`: year of assessment
- `quality`: EEA quality class (Excellent / Good / Sufficient / Poor)
- `bathingWaterType`: coastalBathingWater | inlandBathingWater

## Conventions
- Use dplyr + ggplot2
- Save all plots to plots/ as PNG at 300 dpi
- All analysis scripts source data/load_data.R first
```

Zero tokens spent re-orienting the agent.

# Quarto templates

Reusable YAML so you never set up the same slide twice

---

## The YAML repetition problem

Every new presentation you write this from scratch:

```yaml
---
title: "My Talk"
author: "Peeter"           # ← type this every time
institute: "UT / TalTech"  # ← type this every time
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: dark            # ← set this every time
    slide-number: true     # ← set this every time
    self-contained: true   # ← forget this every time
---
```

**Solution:** a project-level `_quarto.yml` that sets defaults once.

---

## `_quarto.yml` — your personal template

```yaml
# _quarto.yml — copy to any new project folder
author:
  - name: "Peeter"
    affiliation: "University of Tartu / TalTech"
    email: "peeter@ut.ee"

format:
  revealjs:
    theme: dark
    highlight-style: github-dark
    slide-number: true
    transition: slide
    self-contained: true
    logo: assets/ut_logo.svg
    footer: "{{{< meta author >}}} · {{{< meta date >}}}"
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true

execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
```

Any `.qmd` in this project inherits everything. New talks need only:

```yaml
---
title: "My New Talk"
date: today
---
```

# LM Studio

Offline AI — your scripting partner on a plane, in the field, or on an airgapped server

---

## Why run a local LLM?

::: {.incremental}
- **No internet** — airplane, fieldwork, rural server room
- **Privacy** — sensitive data that can't leave your machine
- **No API costs** — unlimited queries once model is downloaded
- **Reproducibility** — pin to a specific model version, forever
:::

---

## LM Studio — what it is

LM Studio is a desktop app + CLI that:

- Downloads models from Hugging Face with one click
- Runs them locally via `llama.cpp` (CPU) or GPU acceleration
- Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API** on `localhost:1234`
- Ships with `lms` — a full command-line interface

**Download:** [lmstudio.ai](https://lmstudio.ai) — Mac, Windows, Linux

---

## Installing the `lms` CLI

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Mac / Linux:**

```bash
# LM Studio app → Install CLI tools
# Or manually:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.lmstudio/bin"

lms --version
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Windows:**

```powershell
# LM Studio app → Install CLI tools
# (adds to user PATH automatically)

lms --version
```
:::
:::

---

## `lms` — essential commands

```bash
lms server start                          # start the API server
lms ls                                    # list downloaded models
lms get "qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct"      # download a model
lms load qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q4_k_m  # load into memory
lms chat                                  # interactive terminal chat
lms status                                # check what's running
lms server stop                           # stop the server
```

---

## Choosing your model — by hardware

| Hardware | Recommended model | Size |
|---|---|---|
| CPU only — Linux / Win | `Phi-4-mini` Q4 | ~2.5 GB |
| CPU only — Linux / Win | `Gemma-3-4B-IT` Q4 | ~3 GB |
| 8 GB VRAM — Linux / Win | `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B` Q4 | ~5 GB |
| 16 GB VRAM — Linux / Win | `Qwen2.5-Coder-14B` Q4 | ~10 GB |
| 24 GB VRAM — Linux / Win | `Mistral-Small-22B` Q4 | ~18 GB |
| Mac 8 GB (M-series) | `Phi-4-mini` Q4 | ~2.5 GB |
| Mac 16 GB (M-series) | `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B` Q4 | ~5 GB |
| Mac 32 GB+ (M-series) | `Qwen2.5-Coder-14B` Q4 | ~10 GB |

::: {.callout-note}
Apple Silicon uses unified memory — a 32 GB MacBook handles what a 32 GB VRAM GPU handles.
**Q4_K_M** is the best quality-per-GB quantisation for all platforms.
:::

---

## Step-by-step: CPU only (Linux / Windows)

```bash
# 1. Install LM Studio from lmstudio.ai, then:
lms server start

# 2. Download a small but capable model (~2.5 GB)
lms get "microsoft/phi-4-mini-instruct-gguf"

# 3. Load it
lms load phi-4-mini-instruct-q4_k_m

# 4. Test in terminal
lms chat
# > Write an R function that reads a CSV and returns
# > summary statistics per numeric column

# 5. Confirm the API is up
curl http://localhost:1234/v1/models
```

Total: ~10 min including download.

---

## Step-by-step: NVIDIA GPU (Linux / Windows)

```bash
# 1. Verify CUDA
nvidia-smi

# 2. Install LM Studio — auto-detects CUDA

# 3. Download coder model (~5 GB)
lms get "qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-gguf"

# 4. Load — offload all layers to GPU
lms load qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q4_k_m \
  --gpu-layers 999

# 5. Chat or query via API
lms chat

# 6. Monitor GPU while running
watch -n1 nvidia-smi
```

---

## Step-by-step: Mac Apple Silicon

```bash
# 1. Install LM Studio (Apple Silicon native — uses Metal)

# 2. Download
lms get "qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-gguf"

# 3. Load (Metal acceleration is automatic)
lms load qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q4_k_m

# 4. Test
lms chat

# 5. Monitor: Activity Monitor → Window → GPU History
```

---

## Using LM Studio with R

LM Studio exposes an OpenAI-compatible API on `localhost:1234`:

```r
library(httr2)

ask_local_llm <- function(prompt, model = "local-model") {
  request("http://localhost:1234/v1/chat/completions") |>
    req_body_json(list(
      model    = model,
      messages = list(list(role = "user", content = prompt))
    )) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json() |>
    (\(r) r$choices[[1]]$message$content)()
}

ask_local_llm("Write a dplyr pipeline to count NAs per column")
```

No API key. No internet. No cost per query.

---

## Using LM Studio with Claude Code offline

Point Claude Code at your local server:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:1234/v1
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=local   # any non-empty string works

claude
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Local models are weaker than Claude — great for focused tasks (fix this function, write a plot) but struggle with complex multi-file reasoning. Use offline; switch back when you have internet.
:::

# Practical exercises

---

## Exercise 1 — Copilot warm-up (10 min)

In RStudio with Copilot enabled:

1. Open a new R script
2. Write this comment — let Copilot complete the rest:

```r
# Load mtcars, fit a linear model of mpg ~ wt + cyl,
# and plot residuals vs fitted values
```

3. **Tab** to accept, **Esc** to reject, **Alt+]** to see alternatives
4. Run the code — does it actually work?

**Goal:** get comfortable with the accept/reject cycle before trusting it.

---

## Exercise 2 — Claude Code session (20 min)

```bash
mkdir ~/ai-exercise && cd ~/ai-exercise
git init && claude
```

Ask Claude to:

1. Create `data/sample.csv` with student grades (name, subject, score)
2. Write `analysis.R` that reads it and produces a summary table
3. Create a ggplot bar chart → `plots/grades.png`
4. Write a `report.qmd` that includes both

**Inspect each file before accepting. Run `git diff` after each edit. Render the QMD.**

---

## Exercise 3 — btw + API key (10 min)

```r
# 1. Add your API key
usethis::edit_r_environ()
# ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...
# Save → restart R

# 2. Verify
Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")

# 3. Use btw with real data

library(palmerpenguins)
penguins_problem <- penguins
penguins_problem$body_mass_g[sample(nrow(penguins), 20)] <- NA
btw(penguins_problem)   # copies to clipboard
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
bw_sample |>
  mutate(quality = factor(quality,
           levels = c("Excellent","Good","Sufficient","Poor"))) |>
  datatable(
    extensions = "Buttons",
    options    = list(
      dom        = "Bfrtip",
      buttons    = list(
        list(extend = "csv",   text = "Download CSV"),
        list(extend = "excel", text = "Download Excel")
      ),
      pageLength = 8,

    backgroundColor = styleEqual(
      names(quality_colours), unname(quality_colours)
    ),
    color = "white", fontWeight = "bold"
  )
```

---

## Demo — interactive map

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
pal <- colorFactor(palette = unname(quality_colours),
                   levels  = names(quality_colours))

leaflet(bw_sample) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.DarkMatter) |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng         = ~lon,
    lat         = ~lat,
    color       = ~pal(quality),
    fillOpacity = 0.85,
    radius      = 9,
    stroke      = FALSE,
    popup       = ~paste0(
      "<b>", site, "</b><br>",
      country, " &middot; ", type, "<br>",
      "<b style='color:", quality_colours[quality], "'>",
      quality, "</b> &middot; ", season
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend("bottomright", pal = pal, values = ~quality,
            title = "Quality", opacity = 0.9)
```

## Exercise 4 — Searchable table with download

A large data frame can be made browsable and downloadable:

```r
library(DT)

bw_ee |>
  select(bathingWaterName, bathingWaterType,
         lon, lat, quality, season) |>
  datatable(
    extensions = "Buttons",
    options = list(
      dom       = "Bfrtip",
      buttons   = c("csv", "excel"),
      pageLength = 15
    ),
    filter    = "top",      # per-column filter boxes
    rownames  = FALSE
  )
```

This renders as an interactive HTML table with search, sort, and download — works in any self-contained `.html` or Shiny app.

---

## Key takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- **Copilot** = inline completion, fast, no project context
- **Claude Code** = agentic, reads files, iterates on errors
- **`btw`** = your live R session as an AI tool — describe only what's needed
- **`CLAUDE.md`** = free persistent project memory for Claude Code
- **`_quarto.yml`** = set your identity and style once, reuse forever
- **LM Studio** = same workflow, offline, weaker model
- **Git first** — always commit before an AI session
:::
